tasks.title: SR latch: the first memory
tasks.statement: Build a latch from two NOR gates cross-coupled: the output of each feeds the input of the other. R is reset, S is set. Wires may go “backwards”: loops are allowed here!
tasks.hint: Two NORs: Q = NOT(R OR nQ), nQ = NOT(S OR Q). Feed S to the gate whose output goes to nQ. Check each step against the list below.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Set: apply S = 1 (R = 0). The latch must output Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Remove the signals: S = 0, R = 0. Q stayed 1: the latch REMEMBERED the bit. That is memory!
spec_text./steps/2/text: Reset: apply R = 1. Q must return to 0, and nQ must rise to 1.
spec_text./steps/3/text: S = 0, R = 0 again: the latch holds 0 until a new command arrives.
spec_text./formula: Q holds the last bit that was set
spec_text./success: You built an SR latch, the simplest memory cell! Feedback (an output returning to an input) is what sets sequential circuits apart from all the previous ones: they remember history. Processor registers are made of such cells.

tasks.title: SR latch from NAND
tasks.statement: The same memory, but built from NAND gates and with “inverted” logic: signals are active LOW. nS = 0 sets Q = 1, nR = 0 resets Q = 0, and idle is nS = nR = 1. Cross-coupled: Q = NAND(nS, nQ), nQ = NAND(nR, Q).
tasks.hint: Two NANDs cross-coupled: feed nS to the gate whose output goes to Q; feed nR to the gate whose output goes to nQ. If NAND is still locked, build it from AND and NOT.

spec_text./steps/1/text: Idle: nS = nR = 1. The latch holds one.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Idle again: the latch holds zero.
spec_text./formula: Q = NAND(nS, nQ); nQ = NAND(nR, Q)
spec_text./success: The NAND latch is the classic: it is built more often than the NOR one. Active low is natural in hardware: chip pins are pulled up to one, and a command is a connection to ground (hence the letter n for negative).

tasks.title: Latch with set priority
tasks.statement: In an ordinary SR latch S = R = 1 is forbidden. Make a latch where SET wins when S = R = 1: Q = 1. One output, Q. Build around a single loop: “Q holds itself while there is no reset”.
tasks.hint: Q = S OR (NOT-R AND Q). Output Q returns to the input of the AND gate; that is the feedback. Three gates: NOT, AND, OR.

spec_text./steps/3/text: Both at once: S = R = 1. Set wins: Q = 1!
spec_text./steps/4/text: Remove S: only R is left, so Q = 0.
spec_text./success: Holding is “Q AND NOT-R” (hold while there is no reset), setting goes through OR (S wins because it is applied last). The order of gates in the chain decides which is stronger, S or R.

tasks.title: Latch with reset priority
tasks.statement: The mirror task: when S = R = 1, RESET wins: Q = 0. Everything else is as in the ordinary latch. Think about where in the chain R must now be “inserted”.
tasks.hint: Now AND comes AFTER OR: Q = NOT-R AND (S OR Q). First “set or hold”, then reset overrides everything.

spec_text./steps/1/text: Both at once: S = R = 1. Reset wins: Q = 0!
spec_text./success: Compare with the previous exercise: the same three gates in a different order, and the priority flipped. The designer has to decide which is stronger; in hardware, “forbidden” states are usually avoided.

tasks.title: SR latch with enable
tasks.statement: Add an enable input E: commands S and R take effect only while E = 1. When E = 0 the latch is locked and keeps its value, whatever happens on S and R.
tasks.hint: Put two AND gates in front of the ordinary NOR-based SR: S' = S·E and R' = R·E. Then cross-couple as in the first exercise of the section. Do not open E while S = R = 1.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Set with E open: S = 1, R = 0, E = 1. Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Lock it: E = 0. The value is stored.
spec_text./steps/2/text: With E locked, apply R = 1: the latch does not react, Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Remove S: R = 1, but E = 0. Q is still 1.
spec_text./steps/4/text: Open E: now R = 1 reaches the latch. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/5/text: Lock E again: the zero is kept.
spec_text./formula: S' = S·E; R' = R·E; then an SR latch
spec_text./success: This is a gated SR latch: the strobe E decides when commands are allowed. The trick, a key on an AND gate before the input, is one you have met already; all synchronous logic rests on it.

tasks.title: Alarm
tasks.statement: A security system: “Sen” is the sensor, “Arm” is the armed mode, “Rst” is reset. Alarm Q turns on only if the sensor fires WHILE ARMED, and stays on even after the sensor goes quiet, until it is reset.
tasks.hint: This is a NOR-based SR latch: S' = Sen·Arm (sensor AND armed), R = Rst. Take Q from the gate that outputs one when set.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Initial reset: Rst = 1. The alarm is off.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Arm the system: Arm = 1, Rst = 0. The sensor is quiet, so all is silent.
spec_text./steps/2/text: The sensor fires: Sen = 1 with Arm = 1. Alarm!
spec_text./steps/3/text: The sensor goes quiet, but the alarm REMEMBERS the trigger: Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/4/text: Reset: Rst = 1. The alarm is off.
spec_text./steps/5/text: Disarm and release reset: Arm = 0, Rst = 0. All quiet.
spec_text./steps/6/text: The sensor fires, but the system is not armed (Arm = 0). No alarm!
spec_text./formula: S' = Sen·Arm; R = Rst; Q is an SR latch
spec_text./success: A typical “flag” circuit: an event sets a bit, and the bit lives until it is cleared. This is how interrupt and status flags work in processors: “did an overflow occur”, “has a message arrived”.

tasks.title: D latch: memory with enable
tasks.statement: Add an enable input E to the latch: while E = 1, output Q follows data D (the latch is “transparent”); when E = 0 the latch “locks” and keeps the stored value.
tasks.hint: Take a NOR-based SR latch and drive it like this: S = D AND E, R = NOT-D AND E. You need two AND gates (or NAND with an inverter), one NOT and two cross-coupled NORs.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Open: E = 1, D = 1. The latch is “transparent”, Q follows D.
spec_text./steps/1/text: Lock it: E = 0 (D is still 1). Q = 1: the value is stored.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Change D to 0 while the latch is locked: Q stays 1. The stored value is kept!
spec_text./steps/3/text: Open E again: now the latch stores D = 0. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/5/text: D = 1 “knocks” on the locked latch, but Q is still 0.
spec_text./formula: E = 1: Q = D; E = 0: Q holds the value
spec_text./success: A D latch is a “gated” memory: while the enable is open, data passes freely, and at the moment of locking it is captured. One step remains to a real flip-flop: make the write happen on the clock EDGE.

tasks.title: D latch from NAND
tasks.statement: The classic D latch circuit: four NANDs (and one inverter on D). Same behavior: E = 1: Q follows D, E = 0: Q holds. But now the “keys” are NANDs and directly act as active low for the latch.
tasks.hint: Two “keys”: s = NAND(D, E) and r = NAND(NOT-D, E). They give active zeros. Then a NAND latch: Q = NAND(s, nQ), nQ = NAND(r, Q).

spec_text./steps/0/text: Open E with D = 0: Q follows D, so Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/1/text: While E = 1, change D to 1: Q follows it “transparently”.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Change D to 0 while E is locked: Q does not react.
spec_text./steps/4/text: Open E again: now Q takes D = 0.
spec_text./formula: s = NAND(D,E); r = NAND(NOT-D,E); Q = NAND(s,nQ); nQ = NAND(r,Q)
spec_text./success: Four NANDs and an inverter make the real D latch from textbooks and old chip series. All the “magic” of memory is two gates cross-coupled plus keys at the input.

tasks.title: D latch with clear
tasks.statement: The D latch gets one more input, CLR (clear). When CLR = 1 the latch is immediately reset to Q = 0 and IGNORES data and enable. When CLR = 0 it is an ordinary D latch (E = 1: follows D, E = 0: holds).
tasks.hint: Strengthen the reset and weaken the set: R' = NOT-D·E OR CLR, S' = D·E·NOT-CLR. Then a NOR-based SR latch. The key “NOT-CLR” turns the set off while the clear is active.

spec_text./steps/2/text: Clear: CLR = 1; even with E locked, the latch is reset. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Release CLR: Q stays 0 (E is still locked).
spec_text./steps/4/text: Open E: the latch writes D = 1 again. Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/5/text: Turn on CLR with E open and D = 1: clear beats data. Q = 0.
spec_text./success: Every register has a clear (reset) input: at power-on a processor zeroes all its state memory with a single signal. It is called “asynchronous” because it acts immediately, without waiting for the enable E.

tasks.title: Two-bit register
tasks.statement: One D latch is not enough: numbers consist of several bits. Build a two-bit register: two D latches with a SHARED enable input E. Data is D1 D0, outputs are Q1 Q0.
tasks.hint: Each bit gets its own D latch from the previous exercises (NOT, two ANDs, two NORs), but both share one enable E: the wire from E goes to the AND gates of both latches.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Write the number 10: D1 = 1, D0 = 0, E = 1.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Change the data to 01; E is locked, so the register still holds 10.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Open E: the register has stored 01.
spec_text./steps/5/text: Data 11 “knocks” on the locked register again. It ignores it.
spec_text./formula: Q1 ← D1 and Q0 ← D0 simultaneously when E = 1
spec_text./success: This is a register already! A processor's word width is just the same latches in a row with a shared write signal: 8, 32 or 64 of them. A single E wire “latches” the whole number at once.

tasks.title: Latch with source selection
tasks.statement: A register often needs to store data from one of two sources. S chooses D0 or D1 (0 → D0, 1 → D1); E = 1 writes the chosen value into the latch. The output is Q.
tasks.hint: Glue two ready-made blocks together: a multiplexer (D0·NOT-S OR D1·S) produces a single value D, followed by a D latch with inputs D and E (two ANDs, NOT, two NORs).

spec_text./steps/0/text: S = 0 selects D0. Open E with D0 = 1: Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Switch S to D1 = 0. The latch is locked and notices nothing: Q = 1.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Open E: now D1 = 0 is written. Q = 0.
spec_text./steps/4/text: While E is open, set D1 = 1: Q follows the selected source “transparently”.
spec_text./formula: D = S ? D1 : D0; latch: E = 1 → Q = D
spec_text./success: There is almost always a multiplexer before a memory input: it chooses WHAT to write (an ALU result, a number from the bus, a constant). Blocks connect the way words connect in a sentence.

tasks.title: Memory cell: write and read
tasks.statement: The finale of the section is a one-bit memory cell. D is data, W is write, R is read. Q is the cell's contents. Out is what the bus sees: Out = Q when R = 1, otherwise 0. Reading must not change the contents.
tasks.hint: The storage is a D latch with enable W (NOT, two ANDs, two NORs). Pass its output Q through an AND gate together with R: this is the “read gate”. Take Q directly from the latch and Out from the gate.

spec_text./steps/0/text: Write a one: D = 1, W = 1, R = 0. Q = 1, and the bus is silent (Out = 0).
spec_text./steps/1/text: Close the write: W = 0. The cell holds 1.
spec_text./steps/2/text: Read: R = 1. A one is placed on the bus: Out = 1.
spec_text./steps/3/text: Change D to 0, but W = 0. The contents do not change, and the bus still sees 1.
spec_text./steps/4/text: Write a zero with read open: W = 1, D = 0. Both the cell and the bus show 0.
spec_text./steps/5/text: Close the write: the cell holds 0, the bus shows 0.
spec_text./formula: Q: latch (W = 1 → Q = D); Out = Q·R
spec_text./success: This is an SRAM cell in miniature: storage, a write input and a read gate. RAM is made of millions of such cells, and the address decoder from the previous section selects which cell opens its W or R.
